explanations.explanation: You got it, baker. Jacob looks up, sees Esau and four hundred men, and splits the children among Leah, Rachel and the two maidservants (Genesis 33:1). Leah and Rachel are Jacob's wives. I think a man in that spot wants his people sorted before anybody says hello.

Close, but the servants aren't what he divides. The text says Jacob divides the children among Leah, Rachel and the two maidservants (Genesis 33:1). The maidservants are in the lineup, but they're part of the groups, not the thing being split. Kids first, friend.

The herds already went ahead as a gift, so they're not what he splits here. What he divides is the children, among Leah, Rachel and the two maidservants (Genesis 33:1). Leah and Rachel are his wives. Four hundred men coming will make a dad count heads, not cattle.

Yes, Rachel, Jacob's wife. She and her son Joseph bring up the very rear (Genesis 33:2). Maidservants and their children go first, Leah and hers next. I think that's a dad putting the ones he holds dearest as far back as he can.

Leah is in the lineup, but she's in the middle. The text puts the maidservants and their children in front, Leah and her children next, and Rachel and Joseph at the rear (Genesis 33:2). Leah is Jacob's wife, and she's neither first nor last. Middle of the line, friend.

Zilpah, Leah's maidservant (Genesis 30:9-10), is out front with the maidservants and their children, not at the back. The very rear belongs to Rachel and her son Joseph (Genesis 33:2). Front of the line and back of the line are about as far apart as you can get. That's a long walk for a mix-up, baker.
That's it. Jacob himself goes on ahead of his whole family (Genesis 33:3). Four hundred men are walking up, and he's the first one they'll meet. That takes nerve, and I think it took every bit of it.

Hiding in the back would be tempting, I'll admit it. But the text says Jacob himself went on ahead, and Rachel and Joseph were the ones at the rear (Genesis 33:2-3). He walked toward his brother first. Not one step toward the back, friend.

explanations.answer: Off to the side with his servants
explanations.explanation: Stepping off to the side is how a man avoids the whole thing. Jacob did the opposite. He went on ahead and bowed to the ground seven times as he approached his brother (Genesis 33:3). He walked right up front, where Esau would see him first.

True, baker. Esau ran to him, embraced him, threw his arms around his neck and kissed him (Genesis 33:4). Jacob is down low bowing, and Esau comes in at a full sprint. Nobody on the planet had that on their bingo card.

It's true, and I know it's hard to believe. The text says Esau ran to Jacob and embraced him, threw his arms around his neck, and kissed him. And they both wept (Genesis 33:4). Jacob had every reason to brace for the worst, and I think that's why this lands so hard.

explanations.answer: God graciously gave them to him
explanations.explanation: Right on. Jacob tells Esau, "These are the children God has graciously given your servant" (Genesis 33:5). He doesn't brag about them. He points to God's grace. And notice he calls himself Esau's servant.

explanations.answer: God gave them as a reward for his work
explanations.explanation: Jacob did work hard for years, but that's not what he says here. He says, "These are the children God has graciously given your servant" (Genesis 33:5). Graciously means a gift, not a paycheck. Jacob keeps the credit with God.

explanations.answer: God sent them to make peace with Esau
explanations.explanation: That's a nice thought, but Jacob never says it. He tells Esau, "These are the children God has graciously given your servant" (Genesis 33:5). The text gives no peace-making job for them. It just says they were given by God's grace.

explanations.answer: To find favor in your sight
explanations.explanation: That's the answer. Jacob says, "To find favor in your sight, my lord" (Genesis 33:8). He calls his brother "my lord," which is quite a change from years before. The gifts are about getting on Esau's good side.

explanations.answer: To repay the debt I owe you
explanations.explanation: Jacob never mentions a debt. When Esau asks about the company, Jacob answers, "To find favor in your sight, my lord" (Genesis 33:8). He wants his brother's favor, not to settle accounts. No ledger comes out in this scene.

explanations.answer: To show the riches in my hand
explanations.explanation: Showing off isn't what Jacob is doing, and he never says so. His answer is, "To find favor in your sight, my lord" (Genesis 33:8). I think a man bowing seven times isn't trying to flash his wealth. He's after his brother's good will.
Not quite, baker. Esau says, "I already have plenty, my brother. Keep what belongs to you" (Genesis 33:9). He turns the gift down first. Jacob has to push before it's accepted (Genesis 33:11).

Right, it's false. Esau says, "I already have plenty, my brother. Keep what belongs to you" (Genesis 33:9). Jacob has to press him before he finally accepts (Genesis 33:11). Two brothers, each insisting the other keep the goods. That's a polite standoff, friend.

True, baker. Jacob says, "I have seen your face, and it is like seeing the face of God, since you have received me favorably" (Genesis 33:10). The reason is right there in his words: Esau welcomed him kindly. A warm welcome from the brother he feared meant a great deal to him.

It's true. Jacob says, "I have seen your face, and it is like seeing the face of God, since you have received me favorably" (Genesis 33:10). The "since" gives the reason in his own words. Esau welcoming him is what he's so grateful for.

explanations.answer: His children are frail and his herds are nursing
explanations.explanation: Yes. Jacob says the children are frail and he must care for sheep and cattle that are nursing their young (Genesis 33:13). Esau's pace would be too much for the little ones. A good dad knows his crew's speed.

explanations.answer: His servants are worn out from the long trip
explanations.explanation: The servants aren't his reason. Jacob points to the children being frail and the sheep and cattle nursing their young (Genesis 33:13). The text says nothing about tired servants. The little ones set the pace.

explanations.answer: His wives need to rest for a few days first
explanations.explanation: Jacob never brings up his wives resting, and he never mentions a few days. What he says is that the children are frail and the animals are nursing their young, and a hard drive for even a day would be too much (Genesis 33:13). The pace is for the little ones, baker.

Seir it is. Jacob says he'll come along slowly "until I come to my lord at Seir" (Genesis 33:14). Seir is the place Esau heads back to (Genesis 33:16). Jacob's promise sounds friendly, and the text then shows him going to Succoth (Genesis 33:17).

Bethel is a real place in Jacob's story (Genesis 28:19), but it's not what he says here. He tells Esau he'll come "until I come to my lord at Seir" (Genesis 33:14). Seir is where Esau goes next (Genesis 33:16).

Hebron is a place in Canaan, but it's not what Jacob names here. He says he'll continue slowly "until I come to my lord at Seir" (Genesis 33:14). Seir is where Esau starts back to that same day (Genesis 33:16). Mixing up place names on a map is easy, friend.

Not this time, baker. Esau offers to leave some of his people, but Jacob replies, "Why do that? Let me find favor in the sight of my lord" (Genesis 33:15). He politely says no. Esau's offer is a kind one, and Jacob still turns it down.

Right. Esau says, "Let me leave some of my people with you," and Jacob answers, "Why do that? Let me find favor in the sight of my lord" (Genesis 33:15). He doesn't take the offer. Esau leaves for Seir that same day (Genesis 33:16).

A house, you got it. Jacob goes on to Succoth, where he builds a house for himself and shelters for his livestock (Genesis 33:17). The animals get shelters too. After all that traveling, I bet that roof felt good.

No tower here. At Succoth, Jacob built a house for himself and shelters for his livestock (Genesis 33:17). Nothing in the text says he built anything tall. A plain house and some animal shelters, friend.

A city wall isn't in the text. Jacob built a house for himself and shelters for his livestock at Succoth (Genesis 33:17). He's setting up a home for his family and animals, not fortifying a town. Walls aren't what this stop is about.
Succoth is right. Jacob built shelters for his livestock there, "that is why the place was called Succoth" (Genesis 33:17). The name comes from what he built. A place named after a barn, baker.

True, baker. Jacob camps just outside Shechem, and the plot where he pitched his tent he bought from the sons of Hamor, Shechem's father (Genesis 33:18-19). The text says he purchased it. He paid for the ground he stood on.

It's true. The plot where Jacob pitched his tent, he purchased from the sons of Hamor, Shechem's father (Genesis 33:19). He camped just outside the city (Genesis 33:18). Hamor's sons sold it, and Jacob bought it.
An altar, yes. There Jacob set up an altar and called it El-Elohe-Israel (Genesis 33:20). He buys the land, then sets up an altar on it. I think that tells you what mattered to him.
Jacob did set up a stone pillar once, at Bethel (Genesis 28:18). Here the text says he set up an altar (Genesis 33:20). Different place, different thing.

No gate in this passage. On the plot he bought, Jacob set up an altar and called it El-Elohe-Israel (Genesis 33:20). He camped outside the city, not at its gate (Genesis 33:18). A gate is for city folks, and Jacob built an altar.
